title: Polycrisis Resilience
subtitle: A Framework for Reducing Human and Systemic Vulnerability in an Era of Interconnected Global Risks
description: Humanity's long-term resilience depends not only on responding to individual crises, but on reducing the underlying vulnerabilities that allow interconnected…
contribution: Establishes the foundational Polycrisis Resilience framework: five structural pillars, four complementary functions, eight development pathways, and a seven-category evaluation architecture for reducing human and systemic vulnerability.
abstract:
Concept developed and originated by Hunter Hughes, Founder of H Heuristics. Polycrisis Resilience is a development-oriented framework for reducing human and systemic vulnerability to interconnected global crises through economic development, technological advancement, institutional strengthening, environmental sustainability, and adaptive capacity.
Rather than treating climate change, environmental pollution, poverty, infectious disease, resource insecurity, geopolitical instability, and economic disruption as isolated shocks, this report formalizes how they interact and demonstrates how coordinated investments in sustainable convergence, technology diffusion, clean development, and preventative governance build durable long-term resilience.

keyFindings.title: Interconnected global risks compound across systems: a direct climate shock of 18.0% can cascade through energy grids, food prices, health burdens, fiscal stress, and institutional strain to produce a 61.0% compounded systemic impact when structural vulnerabilities are high.

Polycrisis Resilience rests on five mutually reinforcing pillars—economic, technological and infrastructural, environmental, human, and institutional resilience—whose cross-pillar empirical correlations range from 0.68 to 0.86 across national income tiers.
The five pillars operationalize four complementary functions: prevention, absorption, adaptation, and recovery.
keyFindings.text: Crucially, recovery must upgrade fragile pre-crisis baselines rather than merely restoring conditions that generated vulnerability.

keyFindings.title: Eight principal development pathways—led by preventative investment (11.0x combined social BCR), clean development (9.7x), and infrastructure development (8.9x)—simultaneously reduce exposure across poverty, health, climate, and fiscal dimensions.

Long-term resilience cannot be separated from development: rising GDP per capita and basic service coverage cut historical disaster mortality from 4.8 per 100,000 in the 1970s to 0.7 in the 2020s, yet billions in the Global South still face acute clean-cooking, PM2.5, and heat gaps.

Evaluating the framework across seven measurable impact categories provides a rigorous empirical scorecard, while explicitly distinguishing intended impact pathways from causal effects that require ongoing empirical evaluation.
